reference.source: Occupational and Environmental Respiratory Medicine reference texts
clinicalPearls: Caused by exposure to talc (hydrated magnesium silicate), either inhaled occupationally (mining, milling, ceramics, cosmetics, rubber) or introduced intravenously
Intravenous talcosis occurs when injection drug users inject crushed oral tablets containing talc filler, producing foreign-body granulomas around vascular deposits
Occupational talc is often contaminated with silica or asbestos fibres, so disease may reflect talco-silicosis or talco-asbestosis rather than pure talc effect
Birefringent talc particles are seen under polarised light within granulomas and giant cells on biopsy
Intravenous disease characteristically causes lower-zone or perihilar micronodularity that may coalesce into masses resembling progressive massive fibrosis
Panacinar lower-zone emphysema is a recognised feature of intravenous talcosis, particularly with methylphenidate injection
Pulmonary hypertension can develop from vascular talc granulomas obstructing small pulmonary arteries
reference.pathophysiology: Talc particles reaching the lung, whether inhaled or delivered intravenously, are engulfed by macrophages and provoke a foreign-body granulomatous reaction with multinucleated giant cells surrounding birefringent crystals. In inhalational disease the particles deposit in airways and interstitium, and any accompanying silica or asbestos amplifies fibrosis. In intravenous talcosis, filler particles lodge in pulmonary arterioles and capillaries, seeding perivascular granulomas that can coalesce into fibrotic conglomerate masses, obliterate the vasculature to cause pulmonary hypertension, and, through mechanisms not fully understood, promote basal panacinar emphysema. Progressive interstitial fibrosis may result from ongoing exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive massive fibrosis from other dusts
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT to define micronodularity, conglomerate masses, and emphysema distribution
Occupational history and, where relevant, a sensitive history of injection drug use
Lung biopsy with polarised-light microscopy demonstrating birefringent talc crystals
Pulmonary function tests and diffusing capacity
Echocardiography or right heart assessment for pulmonary hypertension
redFlags: Progressive pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain
Rapidly enlarging masses requiring exclusion of malignancy
Severe basal emphysema with respiratory failure in injection drug users
Signs of ongoing injection drug use with attendant infective risks
reference.prognosis: Pure occupational talcosis is often indolent, but intravenous talcosis and talc-silicosis can progress to disabling fibrosis, emphysema, pulmonary hypertension, and respiratory failure; cessation of exposure or drug injection is essential to limit progression.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit a history of injection drug use in a patient with unexplained micronodular disease
Attributing conglomerate masses to malignancy without considering talcosis
Assuming occupational talc disease is pure when silica or asbestos contamination is common
Overlooking developing pulmonary hypertension in intravenous talcosis
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Eliminate ongoing exposure by removing the patient from occupational talc and supporting cessation of injection drug use, the essential step to limit progression
Offer addiction support and harm-reduction services where intravenous disease relates to injection of crushed oral tablets
Provide symptomatic support with supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia, bronchodilators and pulmonary rehabilitation
Consider a trial of corticosteroids for progressive granulomatous inflammation, recognising the evidence is limited
Encourage smoking cessation and give influenza and pneumococcal vaccination to protect remaining lung function
Screen for and manage pulmonary hypertension arising from vascular obliteration
Refer advanced fibrotic or emphysematous disease for lung transplantation assessment
Manage through respiratory and occupational lung disease specialists
